1 | /**
2 | _ Content Reference Tool — File Source Resolver
3 | _
4 | _ Resolves content references pointing to files on disk.
5 | _ Supports line range extraction and anchor/selector matching.
6 | _/
7 |
8 | import _ as fs from "fs/promises"
9 | import _ as path from "path"
10 | import type { ContentRef } from "../../../../shared/tools"
11 | import type { SelectorResult } from "../selector"
12 | import { resolveContentRef } from "../selector"
13 | import type { Task } from "../../../task/Task"
14 |
15 | /\*\*
16 | _ Resolve a file source reference by reading the file and matching content.
17 | _
18 | _ Resolution priority:
19 | _ 1. Line range (startLine/endLine) — extracted directly
20 | _ 2. Anchor pair / selector — delegated to resolveContentRef
21 | _
22 | _ @param ref - ContentRef with ref.ref as a relative file path and optional line numbers
23 | _ @param task - Current task instance providing cwd for relative path resolution
24 | _ @returns SelectorResult with the extracted content fragment
25 | _ @throws If file is not found, unreadable, or matching fails
26 | _/
27 | export async function resolveFileSource(ref: ContentRef, task: Task): Promise<SelectorResult> {
28 | // Resolve file path relative to task cwd
29 | const cwd = task.cwd || process.cwd()
30 | const filePath = path.resolve(cwd, ref.ref)
31 |
32 | let content: string
33 | try {
34 | content = await fs.readFile(filePath, "utf-8")
35 | } catch (err) {
36 | throw new Error(
37 | `File not found or unreadable: ${ref.ref} (resolved: ${filePath}). ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : ""}`,
38 | )
39 | }
40 |
41 | // Priority 1: Line range (startLine/endLine)
42 | if (ref.startLine !== undefined) {
43 | const lines = content.split("\n")
44 | const start = Math.max(0, ref.startLine - 1) // 1-based → 0-based
45 | const end = ref.endLine !== undefined ? Math.min(lines.length, ref.endLine) : start + 1
46 |
47 | const extracted = lines.slice(start, end).join("\n")
48 | const sourceId = `file://${filePath}:${ref.startLine}-${ref.endLine ?? ref.startLine}`
49 |
50 | return {
51 | sourceId,
52 | content: extracted,
53 | startOffset: start,
54 | endOffset: end,
55 | confidence: 1.0,
56 | method: "exact",
57 | }
58 | }
59 |
60 | // Priority 2+: Anchor pair / selector
61 | const sourceId = `file://${filePath}`
62 | return resolveContentRef(sourceId, content, ref)
63 | }

1 | /**
2 | _ Content Reference Tool — Terminal Source Resolver
3 | _
4 | _ Resolves content references pointing to command output artifacts
5 | _ stored in the task's command-output directory.
6 | _/
7 |
8 | import _ as fs from "fs/promises"
9 | import \* as path from "path"
10 | import type { ContentRef } from "../../../../shared/tools"
11 | import type { SelectorResult } from "../selector"
12 | import { resolveContentRef } from "../selector"
13 | import type { Task } from "../../../task/Task"
14 | import { getTaskDirectoryPath } from "../../../../utils/storage"
15 |
16 | /**
17 | _ Resolve a terminal source reference by reading a command output artifact.
18 | _
19 | _ Resolution strategy:
20 | _ 1. Direct artifact path: ref.ref = "cmd-xxx.txt"
21 | _ 2. Content fingerprint matching: scan command-output files for startAnchor
22 | _
23 | _ @param ref - ContentRef with ref.ref as artifact filename or startAnchor for fingerprint matching
24 | _ @param task - Current task instance for accessing the command-output directory
25 | _ @returns SelectorResult with the extracted content fragment
26 | _ @throws If task directory is unavailable, artifact not found, or matching fails
27 | _/
28 | export async function resolveTerminalSource(ref: ContentRef, task: Task): Promise<SelectorResult> {
29 | // Get task directory path via provider
30 | const provider = task.providerRef.deref()
31 | const globalStoragePath = provider?.context?.globalStorageUri?.fsPath
32 | if (!globalStoragePath) {
33 | throw new Error("Global storage path not available for terminal source resolution.")
34 | }
35 |
36 | const taskDirPath = await getTaskDirectoryPath(globalStoragePath, task.taskId)
37 |
38 | // Try direct path first (ref.ref = "cmd-xxx.txt")
39 | let artifactPath = path.join(taskDirPath, "command-output", ref.ref)
40 | let content: string | null = null
41 |
42 | try {
43 | content = await fs.readFile(artifactPath, "utf-8")
44 | } catch {
45 | // If ref.ref is empty or not found, try content fingerprint matching
46 | if (!ref.ref && ref.startAnchor) {
47 | // Scan command-output directory for matching files
48 | const outputDir = path.join(taskDirPath, "command-output")
49 | let files: string[]
50 | try {
51 | files = await fs.readdir(outputDir)
52 | } catch {
53 | throw new Error("Command output directory not found.")
54 | }
55 |
56 | // Try to match by first few chars of content (startAnchor can be the command itself)
57 | for (const file of files) {
58 | if (!file.startsWith("cmd-")) continue
59 | const filePath = path.join(outputDir, file)
60 | const fileContent = await fs.readFile(filePath, "utf-8")
61 | if (fileContent.includes(ref.startAnchor)) {
62 | content = fileContent
63 | artifactPath = filePath
64 | break
65 | }
66 | }
67 |
68 | if (content === null) {
69 | throw new Error(`No terminal output found containing: ${ref.startAnchor}`)
70 | }
71 | } else {
72 | throw new Error(`Terminal artifact not found: ${ref.ref}`)
73 | }
74 | }
75 |
76 | const sourceId = `terminal://${path.basename(artifactPath)}`
77 | return resolveContentRef(sourceId, content, ref)
78 | }

1 | /\*\*
2 | _ Content Reference Tool — Tool Source Resolver
3 | _
4 | _ Resolves content references pointing to tool_result blocks in the
5 | _ conversation history. Matches by tool name across tool_use/tool_result pairs.
6 | _/
7 |
8 | import type { ContentRef } from "../../../../shared/tools"
9 | import type { SelectorResult } from "../selector"
10 | import { resolveContentRef } from "../selector"
11 | import type { Task } from "../../../task/Task"
12 |
13 | /**
14 | _ Resolve a tool source reference by finding the last tool_result for a given tool.
15 | _
16 | _ Traverses userMessageContent backwards to find the latest tool_result,
17 | _ then verifies the tool name by matching tool_use_id against assistantMessageContent.
18 | _
19 | _ @param ref - ContentRef with ref.ref as the tool name (e.g., "read_file")
20 | _ @param task - Current task instance with user and assistant message content
21 | _ @returns SelectorResult with the tool result content
22 | _ @throws If no matching tool result is found
23 | _/
24 | export async function resolveToolSource(ref: ContentRef, task: Task): Promise<SelectorResult> {
25 | // Find the last tool_result for the specified tool
26 | const toolName = ref.ref
27 | const messages = task.userMessageContent
28 |
29 | // Traverse backwards to find latest result for this tool
30 | for (let i = messages.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
31 | const block = messages[i]
32 |
33 | if (isToolResultBlock(block)) {
34 | const toolUseId = block.tool_use_id
35 |
36 | // Find the corresponding tool_use in assistant message to match tool name
37 | const assistantMessages = task.assistantMessageContent
38 | for (const msg of assistantMessages) {
39 | if (
40 | (msg.type === "tool_use" || msg.type === "mcp_tool_use") &&
41 | (msg as any).id === toolUseId &&
42 | (msg as any).name === toolName
43 | ) {
44 | // Found matching tool result
45 | const content = extractTextContent(block)
46 | const sourceId = `tool:${toolName}:${toolUseId}`
47 | return resolveContentRef(sourceId, content, ref)
48 | }
49 | }
50 | }
51 | }
52 |
53 | throw new Error(`No tool result found for tool: ${toolName}`)
54 | }
55 |
56 | /**
57 | _ Type guard to check if a user message block is a ToolResultBlockParam.
58 | _/
59 | function isToolResultBlock(block: any): block is { type: "tool_result"; tool_use_id: string; content: any } {
60 | return block && block.type === "tool_result" && typeof block.tool_use_id === "string"
61 | }
62 |
63 | /\*_
64 | _ Extract text content from a tool_result block.
65 | _
66 | _ Handles both string content and structured content arrays.
67 | \*/
68 | function extractTextContent(block: { content: any }): string {
69 | if (typeof block.content === "string") {
70 | return block.content
71 | }
72 | if (Array.isArray(block.content)) {
73 | return block.content
74 | .filter((c: any) => c.type === "text")
75 | .map((c: any) => c.text)
76 | .join("\n")
77 | }
78 | return JSON.stringify(block.content || "")
79 | }

199 | "XML tool calls are no longer supported. Use native tool calling (nativeArgs) instead.",
200 | )
201 | }
202 | throw new Error("Tool call is missing native arguments (nativeArgs).")
203 | }
204 | } catch (error) {
205 | console.error(`Error parsing parameters:`, error)
206 | const errorMessage = `Failed to parse ${this.name} parameters: ${error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}`
207 | await callbacks.handleError(`parsing ${this.name} args`, new Error(errorMessage))
208 | // Note: handleError already emits a tool_result via formatResponse.toolError in the caller.
209 | // Do NOT call pushToolResult here to avoid duplicate tool_result payloads.
210 | return
211 | }
212 |
213 | // Execute with typed parameters
214 | await this.execute(params, task, callbacks)
215 | }
216 | }

217 | /\*\*
218 | _ ContentRef specifies which fragment to cite from session context.
219 | _
220 | _ Priority chain: startLine+endLine > startAnchor+endAnchor > startAnchor > selector

222 | _ For strict mode compliance: ALL properties are required in JSON Schema,
223 | _ but optional ones use `string | null` in TypeScript.

226 | source: ContentSource

228 | _ Source identifier:
229 | _ - for "chat": message index ("-1" = last assistant message)

232 | _ - for "tool": tool name (e.g. "read_file")
233 | _/
234 | ref: string
235 |
236 | // --- Anchor Pair (recommended for fragments >60 chars) ---
237 | /** Start anchor: first 15-40 chars of the target fragment _/
238 | startAnchor?: string
239 | /\*\* End anchor: last 15-40 chars of the target fragment, searched AFTER startAnchor _/
240 | endAnchor?: string
241 |
242 | // --- Full Selector (fallback for fragments <=60 chars) ---
243 | /** Exact substring to find in source \*/
244 | selector?: string
245 |
246 | // --- File-specific: Line range ---
247 | /** Starting line number (1-based, only for source="file") _/
248 | startLine?: number
249 | /\*\* End line number (1-based, only for source="file") _/
250 | endLine?: number
251 |
252 | // --- Source hint ---
253 | /** Hint for boundary expansion heuristics \*/
254 | contextType?: "code" | "command" | "prose" | "markdown" | "diff"
255 | }

 3 | 
 4 | 1. Assess what information you already have and what information you need to proceed with the task.
 5 | 2. Choose the most appropriate tool based on the task and the tool descriptions provided. Assess if you need additional information to proceed, and which of the available tools would be most effective for gathering this information. For example using the list_files tool is more effective than running a command like \`ls\` in the terminal. It's critical that you think about each available tool and use the one that best fits the current step in the task.
6 | 3. If multiple actions are needed, you may use multiple tools in a single message when appropriate, or use tools iteratively across messages. 11 | /**
12 |  * Content Reference (CRT) guidelines.
13 |  *
14 |  * CRT allows the agent to cite existing content from session context
15 |  * instead of regenerating it, saving 80-96% tokens on long fragments.
16 |  */
17 | export const CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES =`
18 | ## Content Reference (Ref)
19 |
20 | You can use \`ref\` parameters to cite content already present in the session context, avoiding redundant generation:
21 |
22 | ### When to use Ref
23 | - **Long fragments (>60 chars):** Use \`startAnchor\` + \`endAnchor\` (15-40 chars each)
24 | The Selector Engine finds everything between them automatically.
25 | Example: \`{ ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", startAnchor: "function foo(", endAnchor: "}" } }\`
26 | - **Short fragments (<=60 chars):** Use \`selector\` (exact substring)
27 | Example: \`{ ref: { source: "file", ref: "src/config.ts", selector: "export const API_URL" } }\`
28 | - **Multi-source composition:** Use \`multi_ref\` with \`join_with\` separator
29 | Example: \`{ multi_ref: [...], transform: { join_with: "\\\\n" } }\`
30 | - **MCP tools:** Use inline \`{{ref:source=chat,ref=-1,startAnchor=...}}\` markers inside strings
31 |
32 | ### Supported Sources
33 | | Source | Ref format | Description |
34 | |--------|-----------|-------------|
35 | | \`chat\` | \`"-1"\` (last message), \`"-2"\` | Previous assistant messages |
36 | | \`file\` | \`"src/file.ts"\` (relative path) | Files on disk |
37 | | \`terminal\` | \`"cmd-xxx.txt"\` (artifact) | Command outputs |
38 | | \`tool\` | \`"read_file"\` (tool name) | Results of previous tool calls |
39 |
40 | ### Transforms (optional pipeline)
41 | Order: \`replace → prepend → wrap_with → append\`
42 | - \`replace\`: { from: "old", to: "new" } — substring replacement
43 | - \`prepend\`: "text before" — add before content
44 | - \`wrap_with\`: "template {content}" — wrap with template
45 | - \`append\`: "text after" — add after content
46 |
47 | ### Important
48 | - \`ref\` is OPTIONAL. If omitted, the tool works as usual.
49 | - If ref fails (content condensed, file changed), the content is regenerated automatically.
50 | - Do NOT use both \`command\` and \`ref\` in the same call — ref has priority.
51 | `

 27 | export class UseMcpToolTool extends BaseTool<"use_mcp_tool"> {
 28 | 	readonly name = "use_mcp_tool" as const
 29 | 
 30 | 	/**
 31 | 	 * Scan string arguments for {{ref:...}} markers and resolve them inline.
 32 | 	 * This enables CRT for MCP tools whose schemas we don't control.
 33 | 	 */
 34 | 	private async injectRefsIntoArgs(args: Record<string, unknown>, task: Task): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
 35 | 		const resolved: Record<string, unknown> = {}
 36 | 
 37 | 		for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(args)) {
 38 | 			if (typeof value === "string") {
 39 | 				resolved[key] = await this.resolveInlineRefs(value, task)
 40 | 			} else if (value !== null && typeof value === "object") {
 41 | 				// Recursively process nested objects
 42 | 				resolved[key] = await this.injectRefsIntoArgs(value as Record<string, unknown>, task)
 43 | 			} else {
 44 | 				resolved[key] = value
 45 | 			}
 46 | 		}
 47 | 
 48 | 		return resolved
 49 | 	}
 50 | 
 51 | 	/**
 52 | 	 * Resolve all {{ref:...}} markers within a single string.
 53 | 	 * Pattern: {{ref:source=chat,ref=-1,startAnchor=...,endAnchor=...}}
 54 | 	 */
 55 | 	private readonly REF_PATTERN = /\{\{ref:(.*?)\}\}/
 56 | 
 57 | 	private async resolveInlineRefs(text: string, task: Task): Promise<string> {
 58 | 		if (!this.REF_PATTERN.test(text)) {
 59 | 			return text
 60 | 		}
 61 | 
 62 | 		let result = text
 63 | 		let match: RegExpExecArray | null
 64 | 
 65 | 		// Reset lastIndex
 66 | 		this.REF_PATTERN.lastIndex = 0
 67 | 
 68 | 		while ((match = this.REF_PATTERN.exec(result)) !== null) {
 69 | 			const fullMatch = match[0]
 70 | 			const paramsStr = match[1]
 71 | 
 72 | 			// Parse key=value pairs from the ref string
 73 | 			const params: Record<string, string> = {}
 74 | 			for (const part of paramsStr.split(",")) {
 75 | 				const eqIdx = part.indexOf("=")
 76 | 				if (eqIdx === -1) continue
 77 | 				const k = part.slice(0, eqIdx).trim()
 78 | 				const v = part.slice(eqIdx + 1).trim()
 79 | 				params[k] = v
 80 | 			}
 81 | 
 82 | 			try {
 83 | 				const content = await resolveRef(
 84 | 					{
 85 | 						ref: {
 86 | 							source: (params.source || "chat") as ContentSource,
 87 | 							ref: params.ref || "-1",
 88 | 							startAnchor: params.startAnchor,
 89 | 							endAnchor: params.endAnchor,
 90 | 							selector: params.selector,
 91 | 						},
 92 | 					},
 93 | 					task,
 94 | 				)
 95 | 
 96 | 				result = result.replace(fullMatch, content.content)
 97 | 			} catch (error) {
 98 | 				// Graceful fallback: keep the ref marker as-is so model sees failure
 99 | 				console.error(`[CRT] Failed to resolve inline ref: ${fullMatch}`, error)
100 | }
101 | }
102 |
103 | return result
104 | }

      import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest"
      import { resolveSelector, resolveAnchorPair, resolveContentRef } from "../selector"
      import type { ContentRef } from "../../../../shared/tools"

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Fixtures
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

const SOURCE_CODE = `function greet(name: string): string {
	const greeting = \`Hello, \${name}!\`
return greeting
}

function farewell(name: string): void {
const message = \`Goodbye, \${name}!\`
console.log(message)
}`

const SOURCE_PROSE = `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
This is a test sentence with some punctuation!
Smart quotes: \u201CHello\u201D and em-dash\u2014like this.
Multiple    spaces    to    collapse.`

const SOURCE_UNICODE = `Русский текст с разными символами.
日本語のテキストです。
Emoji: 🚀🔥🎉`

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Helper: create minimal ContentRef
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

function makeRef(overrides: Partial<ContentRef> & { ref: string; source: "chat" | "file" | "terminal" | "tool" }): ContentRef {
return {
startAnchor: undefined,
endAnchor: undefined,
selector: undefined,
startLine: undefined,
endLine: undefined,
contextType: undefined,
...overrides,
}
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// resolveSelector
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

describe("resolveSelector", () => {
describe("Stage 1 — Exact Match", () => {
it("finds an exact substring in source code", () => {
const result = resolveSelector("code", SOURCE_CODE, "Hello")
expect(result.content).toBe("Hello")
expect(result.method).toBe("exact")
expect(result.confidence).toBe(1.0)
expect(result.startOffset).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)
expect(result.sourceId).toBe("code")
})

    	it("returns line number for exact match", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("code", SOURCE_CODE, "function farewell")
    		expect(result.line).toBe(6)
    		expect(result.content).toContain("function farewell")
    	})
    })

    describe("Stage 2 — Normalized Match", () => {
    	it("matches despite whitespace differences", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("prose", SOURCE_PROSE, "Multiple spaces to collapse")
    		expect(result.method).toBe("normalized")
    		expect(result.confidence).toBe(0.9)
    		expect(result.content).toContain("Multiple")
    	})

    	it("matches with smart quotes normalized to straight quotes", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("prose", SOURCE_PROSE, "\"Hello\"")
    		expect(result.method).toBe("normalized")
    		expect(result.confidence).toBe(0.9)
    		expect(result.content).toContain("Hello")
    	})

    	it("matches when punctuation is normalized (em-dash)", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("prose", SOURCE_PROSE, "em-dash-like this")
    		expect(result.method).toBe("normalized")
    		expect(result.content).toContain("em-dash")
    	})
    })

    describe("Stage 3 — LCS Fuzzy Match", () => {
    	it("finds content with minor typos (80% tolerance)", () => {
    		const source = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
    		const result = resolveSelector("fuzzy", source, "The quick brown fox jumps", { tolerance: 0.2 })
    		expect(result.method).toBe("fuzzy")
    		expect(result.confidence).toBe(0.7)
    		expect(result.content).toContain("quick brown fox")
    	})

    	it("matches with character-level differences within tolerance", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("fuzzy", SOURCE_CODE, "function farewell(name: string) {")
    		// Should match via fuzzy since the exact has "void" not inferred
    		expect(result.method).toBe("fuzzy")
    		expect(result.confidence).toBe(0.7)
    	})

    	it("fails when below minimum match length", () => {
    		const source = "abc"
    		expect(() => resolveSelector("fail", source, "xyz", { tolerance: 0.1 })).toThrow()
    	})

    	it("rejects empty source gracefully", () => {
    		expect(() => resolveSelector("empty", "", "anything")).toThrow("Empty source")
    	})

    	it("rejects empty quote gracefully", () => {
    		expect(() => resolveSelector("empty", "source", "")).toThrow("Empty quote")
    	})
    })

    describe("Stage 4 — Word-Boundary Expansion", () => {
    	it("expands partial word match to word boundaries", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("expand", SOURCE_CODE, "greet", { expandToWords: true })
    		// "greet" is a word boundary itself, so it shouldn't expand
    		expect(result.content).toBe("greet")
    	})

    	it("does NOT expand when expandToWords is false", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("noexpand", SOURCE_CODE, "greet", { expandToWords: false })
    		expect(result.content).toBe("greet")
    	})
    })

    describe("Case Sensitivity", () => {
    	it("matches case-insensitively by default", () => {
    		const result = resolveSelector("code", SOURCE_CODE, "HELLO")
    		expect(result.method).toBe("exact") // because we lowercased
    	})

    	it("fails case-sensitive match when case differs", () => {
    		expect(() => resolveSelector("code", SOURCE_CODE, "HELLO", { caseSensitive: true })).toThrow()
    	})
    })

})

it("resolves content between startAnchor and endAnchor", () => {

expect(result.method).toBe("anchor")
expect(result.content).toContain("function greet")

expect(result.content).toContain("Hello")

})

})

    		expect(() => resolveContentRef("empty", "", ref)).toThrow("Empty source")
    	})

Ты находишься в проекте Roo Code, в директории `/home/agi/PROGRAMMS/Zoo-Code`. Проект — VS Code extension для AI-агента. Мы реализовали CRT (Content Reference Tool) модуль.

Создать файл `src/core/tools/ref/__tests__/transform.spec.ts` с полными unit-тестами для модуля `src/core/tools/ref/transform.ts`.

### Исходный код transform.ts:

```typescript
export interface TransformOptions {
	replace?: { from: string; to: string } | null
	prepend?: string | null
	wrap_with?: string | null
	append?: string | null
	join_with?: string | null
}

export function applyTransform(content: string, transform?: TransformOptions | null): string {
	if (!content || !transform) {
		return content
	}
	let result = content
	// Step 1: replace
	if (transform.replace && transform.replace.from) {
		if (result.includes(transform.replace.from)) {
			result = result.split(transform.replace.from).join(transform.replace.to)
		}
	}
	// Step 2: prepend
	if (transform.prepend) {
		result = transform.prepend + result
	}
	// Step 3: wrap_with
	if (transform.wrap_with) {
		const placeholder = "{content}"
		if (transform.wrap_with.includes(placeholder)) {
			result = transform.wrap_with.replace(placeholder, result)
		} else {
			result = transform.wrap_with + result
		}
	}
	// Step 4: append
	if (transform.append) {
		result = result + transform.append
	}
	return result
}

export function applyMultiTransform(
	contents: string[],
	transform?: TransformOptions | null,
): { contents: string[]; joined?: string } {
	if (!contents || contents.length === 0 || !transform) {
		return { contents }
	}
	const transformed = contents.map((c) => applyTransform(c, transform))
	let joined: string | undefined
	if (transform.join_with) {
		joined = transformed.join(transform.join_with)
	}
	return { contents: transformed, joined }
}
```

### Требования к тестам:

1. **applyTransform** — все 4 шага pipeline (replace → prepend → wrap_with → append):
    - Каждый шаг изолированно
    - Все 4 шага вместе (проверить порядок)
    - replace без совпадения (from не найден) → replace пропускается, остальные применяются
    - empty content → возврат as-is
    - null/undefined transform → возврат as-is
    - wrap_with с {content} placeholder → content вставляется
    - wrap_with без {content} → content дописывается в конец
    - replace.all — замена всех вхождений
2. **applyMultiTransform** — множественные фрагменты:
    - Каждый фрагмент трансформируется независимо
    - join_with соединяет фрагменты
    - Пустой массив → возврат as-is
    - Без transform → возврат as-is
3. **Edge cases:**
    - Пустые строки
    - Спецсимволы
    - Многострочный контент

- Использовать `vitest` (describe/it/expect — глобально доступны)

Message: ## Задача: Создать unit-тесты для CRT Source Resolvers и resolveRef оркестратора

### Контекст

Ты находишься в проекте Roo Code (директория `/home/agi/PROGRAMMS/Zoo-Code`). Нужно создать тесты для CRT-модулей.

### Файлы для тестирования

**1. Source Resolvers** — `src/core/tools/ref/sources/`:

- `chat.ts` — resolveChatSource: индексирует `task.assistantMessageContent` по отрицательным индексам
- `file.ts` — resolveFileSource: читает файл через `fs.readFile`, затем resolveContentRef
- `terminal.ts` — resolveTerminalSource: ищет artifact в `command-output` директории
- `tool.ts` — resolveToolSource: ищет последний tool_result для заданного tool name

**2. resolveRef оркестратор** — `src/core/tools/ref/index.ts`:

- dispatches to correct source resolver based on `ref.source`
- applies transform pipeline via `applyMultiTransform`
- возвращает `ResolveRefResult`

### Что нужно сделать

Создать ДВА тестовых файла:

#### Файл 1: `src/core/tools/ref/__tests__/sources.spec.ts`

Протестировать все 4 source resolver'а с mocked Task.

**Chat Resolver тесты:**

- Успешное разрешение по индексу "-1" (последнее сообщение)
- Успешное разрешение по индексу "-2"
- TextContent сообщение
- ToolUse сообщение (проверить stringify nativeArgs)
- McpToolUse сообщение
- Ошибка: невалидный индекс (0, положительное число, NaN)
- Ошибка: индекс вне диапазона
- Ошибка: пустое сообщение

**File Resolver тесты:**

- Успешное чтение файла (мокать `fs.readFile`)
- Разрешение с startLine/endLine (line range)
- Ошибка: файл не найден
- Ошибка: selector не найден в файле

**Terminal Resolver тесты:**

- Чтение artifact по прямому пути
- Content fingerprint matching (startAnchor ищется по файлам)
- Ошибка: global storage path недоступен
- Ошибка: artifact не найден

**Tool Resolver тесты:**

- Поиск последнего tool_result для указанного tool
- String content в tool_result
- Array content в tool_result
- Ошибка: tool не найден
- Проверка корректного matching tool_use_id

#### Файл 2: `src/core/tools/ref/__tests__/index.spec.ts`

Протестировать resolveRef оркестратор.

**Тесты:**

- resolveRef с refMeta.ref (single ref) — диспатчится на правильный source resolver
- resolveRef с refMeta.multi_ref (multiple refs) — все разрешаются
- Применение transform pipeline к результатам
- join_with в multi_ref
- Confidence: минимальная из всех resolved fragments
- Ошибка: ни ref, ни multi_ref не указаны
- Ошибка: неизвестный source type

### Важные замечания по реализации:

1. **Task mock:** Source resolvers принимают `Task` объект. Тебе нужно создать mock Task с необходимыми полями. Task имеет:

    - `task.assistantMessageContent: ClineMessage[]` — для chat resolver
    - `task.userMessageContent: ClineMessage[]` — для tool resolver
    - `task.cwd: string` — для file resolver
    - `task.providerRef: { deref(): any }` — для terminal resolver
    - `task.taskId: string` — для terminal resolver

    Создай простой mock-объект, не импортируя реальный Task.

2. **ClineMessage типы (для справки):**

    - `{ type: "text", content: string, partial: boolean }` — TextContent
    - `{ type: "tool_use", name: string, id: string, params/nativeArgs: any }` — ToolUse
    - `{ type: "mcp_tool_use", name: string, arguments: any }` — McpToolUse
    - `{ type: "tool_result", tool_use_id: string, content: string | Array<{type: string, text: string}> }`

3. **Мокание внешних зависимостей:**

    - `fs.readFile` — используй `vi.mock("fs/promises")` или `vi.spyOn(fs, "readFile")`
    - `fs.readdir` — аналогично
    - `src/utils/storage` — замокай `getTaskDirectoryPath`

4. **Формат тестов:** vitest, глобальные describe/it/expect. Все комментарии на английском.

### Проверка

После создания файлов, проверь что тесты запускаются:

cd /home/agi/PROGRAMMS/Zoo-Code/src && npx vitest run core/tools/ref/__tests__/index.spec.ts
```

**Исходный код** (из `src/core/tools/BaseTool.ts`):

```typescript
private injectRefContent(params, toolName, refResults): ToolParams {
    const p = { ...params } as any
    const content = refResults.joined ?? refResults.content
    switch (toolName) {
        case "execute_command": p.command = content; break
        case "write_to_file": p.content = content; break
        case "apply_diff": p.diff = content; break
        case "apply_patch": p.patch = content; break
        case "edit":
        case "search_and_replace":
        case "search_replace":
        case "edit_file":
            p.new_string = content; break
    }
    return p
}
```

**Тесты для injectRefContent:**

- execute_command → подставляет content в `command`
- write_to_file → подставляет content в `content`
- apply_diff → подставляет content в `diff`
- apply_patch → подставляет content в `patch`
- edit → подставляет content в `new_string`
- search_and_replace → подставляет content в `new_string`
- search_replace → подставляет content в `new_string`
- edit_file → подставляет content в `new_string`
- joined имеет приоритет над content (когда joined задан)
- Неизвестный tool name → params возвращаются без изменений
- Исходные params НЕ мутируются (создаётся копия)

**Тесты для handle() CRT-интеграцию:**

- Когда block.refMeta задан и resolveRef успешен → params обновляются
- Когда block.refMeta задан и resolveRef падает → graceful fallback (оригинальные params)
- Когда block.refMeta не задан → CRT пропускается
- Когда block.nativeArgs не задан → ошибка "missing nativeArgs"

Message: ## Задача: Создать интеграционный тест CRT (Content Reference Tool)

### Контекст

Ты в проекте Roo Code (`/home/agi/PROGRAMMS/Zoo-Code`). Реализован модуль CRT (Content Reference Tool) — механизм цитирования контента внутри AI-агента. Нужно создать **реальный интеграционный тест**, который проверяет end-to-end сценарии использования CRT.

### Где создать

Файл: `src/core/tools/ref/__tests__/crt-integration.spec.ts`

### Что тестировать

Интеграционный тест должен проверить **сквозные сценарии** от refMeta → через resolveRef → через source resolvers → через selector engine → через transform engine → до финального результата. Без моков на уровень selector/transform, но с моками на внешние зависимости (fs, task).

### Сценарии (минимум 10):

1. **Single ref: chat source + exact selector**

    - ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", selector: "function greet" }
    - Проверить: resolveRef возвращает content с "function greet"

2. **Single ref: chat source + anchor pair**

    - ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", startAnchor: "function greet", endAnchor: "return" }
    - Проверить: content содержит всё между anchors

3. **Single ref: chat source + normalized match**

    - ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", selector: "Function Greet" }
    - Проверить: whitespace normalization, confidence 0.9

4. **Single ref: chat source + fuzzy match (tolerance)**

    - ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", selector: "functoin greet" (typo) }
    - Проверить: LCS fuzzy match, confidence 0.7

5. **multi_ref из 2 фрагментов + join_with**

    - multi_ref: [{source:"chat",ref:"-1",selector:"function greet"}, {source:"chat",ref:"-2",selector:"function farewell"}]
    - transform: { join_with: "\n---\n" }
    - Проверить: joined содержит оба фрагмента через разделитель

6. **multi_ref + transform pipeline (replace + prepend + wrap + append)**

    - multi_ref с 1 ref + полный transform pipeline
    - Проверить: applyTransform вызывается в правильном порядке

7. **multi_ref + mixed fragment transforms**

    - Каждый фрагмент трансформируется независимо перед join
    - Проверить: содержимое каждого фрагмента изменено

8. **Confidence aggregation**

    - multi_ref где один ref имеет confidence 0.7 (fuzzy), другой 1.0 (exact)
    - Проверить: итоговый confidence = 0.7 (минимум)

9. **File source (mocked fs)**

    - ref: { source: "file", ref: "test.ts", startLine: 1, endLine: 3 }
    - Мокать fs.readFile чтобы вернуть тестовый контент
    - Проверить: resolveRef возвращает строки 1-3

10. **Terminal source (mocked fs)**

    - ref: { source: "terminal", ref: "cmd-output.txt" }
    - Мокать fs.readFile + путь через getTaskDirectoryPath
    - Проверить: контент из artifact

11. **Error handling — graceful fallback через BaseTool**

    - ref с неверным selector
    - Проверить: resolveRef выбрасывает ошибку
    - Проверить: BaseTool.handle() ловит ошибку и не прерывает выполнение

12. **Edge case: empty multi_ref**

    - multi_ref: []
    - Проверить: resolveRef выбрасывает ошибку "No ref or multi_ref"

13. **Edge case: transform without multi_ref (single ref + transform)**

    - ref + transform.prepend
    - Проверить: prepend применяется к контенту

14. **Real content extraction** — полный pipeline:
    - Сообщение: длинная строка кода
    - ref: source "chat", ref "-1", selector "const greeting"
    - transform: { prepend: "// RESULT:\n", append: "\n// END" }
    - Проверить: финальный content содержит prepend + original + append

### План реализации

1. Используй `vi.mock()` для:

    - `fs/promises` — для file и terminal source
    - `../../../../utils/storage` — для terminal source
    - `../../../task/Task` — не мокай, сделай mock Task объекта

2. Создай **один общий Task mock** со структурой:

    ```typescript
    const taskMock = {
    	cwd: "/test/project",
    	taskId: "test-task-id",
    	providerRef: { deref: () => ({ context: { globalStorageUri: { fsPath: "/test/storage" } } }) },
    	assistantMessageContent: [
    		{
    			type: "text",
    			content:
    				"function greet(name: string): string {\n  const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`\n  return greeting\n}",
    			partial: false,

3. Для мока `fs`:

4. Импортируй `resolveRef` из `../index` для прямых тестов оркестратора
5. Импортируй `BaseTool` для теста graceful fallback

### Важно:

- Тесты НЕ должны мокать selector.ts, transform.ts — они тестируются на реальных функциях
- Только fs/promises и storage мокаются

    - Проверить: whitespace normalization, confidence 0.9

7. **multi_ref + mixed fragment transforms**

### Вариант B — Если автоматическое обновление не сработает

```
## Content Reference (Ref)

You can use `ref` parameters to cite content already present in the session context, avoiding redundant generation:

### When to use Ref
- **Long fragments (>60 chars):** Use `startAnchor` + `endAnchor` (15-40 chars each)
  The Selector Engine finds everything between them automatically.
  Example: `{ ref: { source: "chat", ref: "-1", startAnchor: "function foo(", endAnchor: "}" } }`
- **Short fragments (<=60 chars):** Use `selector` (exact substring)
  Example: `{ ref: { source: "file", ref: "src/config.ts", selector: "export const API_URL" } }`
- **Multi-source composition:** Use `multi_ref` with `join_with` separator
  Example: `{ multi_ref: [...], transform: { join_with: "\\\\n" } }`
- **MCP tools:** Use inline `{{ref:source=chat,ref=-1,startAnchor=...}}` markers inside strings

### Supported Sources
| Source | Ref format | Description |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| `chat` | `"-1"` (last message), `"-2"` | Previous assistant messages |
| `file` | `"src/file.ts"` (relative path) | Files on disk |
| `terminal` | `"cmd-xxx.txt"` (artifact) | Command outputs |
| `tool` | `"read_file"` (tool name) | Results of previous tool calls |

### Transforms (optional pipeline)
Order: `replace → prepend → wrap_with → append`
- `replace`: { from: "old", to: "new" } — substring replacement
- `prepend`: "text before" — add before content
- `wrap_with`: "template {content}" — wrap with template
- `append`: "text after" — add after content

### Important
- `ref` is OPTIONAL. If omitted, the tool works as usual.
- If ref fails (content condensed, file changed), the content is regenerated automatically.
- Do NOT use both `command` and `ref` in the same call — ref has priority.
```

describe("Stage 3 — LCS Fuzzy Match", () => {

// "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy doG" has 1 wrong char (G≠g)
// With caseSensitive: true, exact/normalized fail → LCS matches 41/42 chars (97.6%) ≥ 80% → fuzzy
const result = resolveSelector("fuzzy", source, "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy doG", { tolerance: 0.2, caseSensitive: true })
expect(result.method).toBe("fuzzy")
expect(result.confidence).toBe(0.7)
expect(result.content).toContain("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
})

18 | ## Content Reference (Ref)

20 | You can use \`ref\` parameters to cite content already present in the session context, avoiding redundant generation:

22 | ### When to use Ref
23 | - **Long fragments (>60 chars):** Use \`startAnchor\` + \`endAnchor\` (15-40 chars each)
24 | The Selector Engine finds everything between them automatically.

27 | Example: \`{ ref: { source: "file", ref: "src/config.ts", selector: "export const API_URL" } }\`

## 1️⃣ Где инжектится CRT-промпт?

Одна строка в [`src/core/prompts/system.ts:94`](src/core/prompts/system.ts:94):

```typescript
const basePrompt = `${roleDefinition}
...
${getToolUseGuidelinesSection()}

${CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES}      // ← вот здесь

${getCapabilitiesSection(cwd, ...)}
...
`
```

CRT — это **часть system prompt'а**, такая же как секция `CAPABILITIES` или `MODES`. Она статическая константа в [`src/core/prompts/sections/tool-use-guidelines.ts:17`](src/core/prompts/sections/tool-use-guidelines.ts:17), экспортируется через [`sections/index.ts:11`](src/core/prompts/sections/index.ts:11) и импортируется в `system.ts`.

---

## 2️⃣ Как часто инжектится?

**Один раз за задачу.**

System prompt генерируется в `SYSTEM_PROMPT()` при создании нового `Task` и передаётся в API как `system_message`. Он **кешируется на всю длительность задачи** и не перегенеривается при каждом tool call.

Это значит:

- **1 инъекция на таск** = на 1-10-100 шагов модели
- Секция ~150 токенов платится **один раз**, независимо от того, сколько раз модель использует `ref`
- Если модель НЕ использует CRT — ~150 токенов потрачены впустую на старте

> **Аналогия**: это как иметь в system prompt'е инструкцию «ты можешь использовать ножницы», даже если ты режешь бумагу каждый шаг. Сами ножницы (инструкция) — разово, резка (реальные `ref`) — на каждом шаге, где они нужны.

---

## 3️⃣ Точный размер

Подсчёт секции `CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES`:

| Метрика                         | Значение         |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| Символов                        | ~600             |
| Строк                           | 35               |
| Слов                            | ~120             |
| Токенов (GPT-4, ~0.25 tok/char) | **~150 токенов** |

Для сравнения:

| Секция                          |   Размер (токенов)   |
| ------------------------------- | :------------------: |
| `getToolUseGuidelinesSection()` |         ~100         |
| `CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES`  |       **~150**       |
| `getCapabilitiesSection()`      |       ~200-400       |
| `markdownFormattingSection()`   |         ~80          |
| `getModesSection()`             | dep. на кол-во модов |

CRT-секция — **одна из самых компактных** в system prompt'е. Примерно **1-2% от всего system prompt'а** (типичный system prompt — 8000-15000 токенов).

---

## 4️⃣ Экономический анализ

### Когда CRT экономит токены

CRT окупается, когда модель хотя бы **1 раз за задачу** использует `ref` для цитирования фрагмента **длиннее 150 токенов**.

**Формула точки безубыточности:**

```
экономия = (длина_фрагмента × частота_использования) - 150 (стоимость CRT-секции) - (длина_ref_params × частота)
```

Графически:

```
         ▲
         │
Экономия │    📈 использует ref ≥2 раз
         │       за задачу
         │
   0 ────┼──────────────────────────►
         │    📉  использует ref
   -150  │        0-1 раз за задачу
         │
```

### Сценарии

| Сценарий                                   |                Использование CRT                 |  Итого (токенов)   |
| ------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------: | :----------------: |
| Модель никогда не использует `ref`         |            **-150** (плата за промпт)            |     **Потеря**     |
| Модель цитирует 1 фрагмент 200 токенов     | -150 (промпт) - 50 (ref params) + 200 (экономия) | **0** (безубыток)  |
| Модель цитирует 3 фрагмента по 500 токенов |          -150 + 3×(-50) + 3×500 = 1350           | **🔥 massive win** |
| apply_diff c diff из предыдущего ответа    |        -150 - 40 + 400 = **+210 токенов**        |    **Выгодно**     |
| multi_ref 5 фрагментов по 200 токенов      |       -150 - 80 + 1000 = **+770 токенов**        | **Очень выгодно**  |

### Где экономия максимальна

1. **apply_diff** — diff-ы длиной 200-2000 токенов. Огромная экономия при цитировании diff из предыдущего шага.
2. **write_to_file** — содержимое файлов 50-5000 строк. Максимальная экономия, если файл уже был прочитан.
3. **execute_command** — длинные shell-команды из предыдущих вызовов.
4. **edit/search_replace** — new_string может быть длинным.

### Где минимальна

1. execute_command с короткими командами (`npm run build`)
2. apply_diff c очень коротким diff
3. Задачи из 1-2 шагов, где CRT-секция не успевает окупиться

---

## 5️⃣ Архитектурное решение: почему часть system prompt, а не динамическая?

Было 3 варианта:

| Вариант                                                     |                 Размер                 |     Частота     |           Риск            |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------: | :-------------: | :-----------------------: |
| **A. System prompt** (сделано)                              |            **~150 токенов**            |    **1 раз**    | Модель может игнорировать |
| B. Tool description каждой схемы                            | ~40 токенов × 7 схем = **280 токенов** | Каждый API call |       Дублирование        |
| C. Динамический промпт через `CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES` |              ~150 токенов              |   Каждый шаг    |        Жор токенов        |

Выбрали **A** — компактнее всего при долгих задачах, не дублируется в 7 схемах, достаточно для обучения модели.

---

## 6️⃣ Есть ли риск, что модель будет игнорировать?

**Да, есть.** Это стандартная проблема system prompt'ов — модель может:

1. Полностью игнорировать CRT-секцию (продолжать писать полный контент).
2. Использовать неправильный формат `ref` — но graceful fallback в `BaseTool` это переживёт.
3. Перепутать `selector` с `startAnchor` — разные типы поиска.

**Митигация**: graceful fallback в `BaseTool.handle()` (строки 175-186) — если resolveRef падает, инструмент выполняется с оригинальными параметрами. Модель даже не узнает об ошибке — увидит только что контент был сгенерирован полностью.

---

## 7️⃣ Итоговая оценка

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CRT Pricing                                     │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Место:         system prompt                    │
│ Частота:       1 раз / задача                   │
│ Размер:        ~150 токенов                     │
│ Безубыток:     ≥1 цитирования >150 токенов     │
│ Окупаемость:   100% за задач >5-10 шагов       │
│ Риск:          модель может игнорировать        │
│ Безопасность:  graceful fallback                │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

CRT-секция — это **страховка на ~150 токенов**, которая открывает модель к возможности экономить 80-96% токенов на каждом цитировании. В долгих задачах (10+ tool call'ов) это даёт **потенциальную экономию 30-50% входных токенов**.

Result: ## 📊 CRT-промптинг: полный анализ

### Где и как часто

CRT-секция (`CONTENT_REFERENCE_GUIDELINES`) находится в **system prompt'е** — файл [`src/core/prompts/system.ts:94`](src/core/prompts/system.ts:94). Она статическая константа из [`src/core/prompts/sections/tool-use-guidelines.ts:17`](src/core/prompts/sections/tool-use-guidelines.ts:17).

**Инжектируется 1 раз за задачу** — при генерации system prompt'а в `SYSTEM_PROMPT()`. Не перегенерируется при каждом tool call'е. Это значит ~150 токенов платится единожды, независимо от того, сколько шагов сделает модель.

### Размер

| Метрика                  | Значение         |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- |
| Символов                 | ~600             |
| Строк                    | 35               |
| Токенов (~0.25 tok/char) | **~150 токенов** |
| Доля system prompt'а     | ~1-2%            |

### Окупаемость

**Формула экономии:**

```
экономия = (длина_фрагмента × частота) - 150 (CRT-секция) - (длина_ref_params × частота)
```

| Сценарий                              |            Экономия             |
| ------------------------------------- | :-----------------------------: |
| 0 использований `ref`                 | **-150 токенов** (не окупилось) |
| 1 × цитирование 200 токенов           |       **~0** (безубыток)        |
| 3 × цитирование по 500 токенов        |      **+1350 токенов** 🔥       |
| apply_diff c diff из предыдущего шага |        **+210 токенов**         |
| multi_ref 5 × 200 токенов             |        **+770 токенов**         |

**Вывод:** CRT окупается при ≥1 цитировании фрагмента длиннее 150 токенов за задачу. В долгих задачах (10+ шагов) — потенциальная экономия 30-50% входных токенов.

### Риски

Модель может **игнорировать** CRT-секцию — продолжать писать полный контент. Но это не страшно: graceful fallback в [`BaseTool.ts:175-186`](src/core/tools/BaseTool.ts:175) перехватывает любые ошибки `resolveRef` и выполняет инструмент с оригинальными параметрами без уведомления модели.

### Почему system prompt, а не tool description?

- **System prompt** (~150 токенов × **1 раз** за задачу) — текущее решение
- Tool descriptions (~40 × 7 = 280 токенов × **каждый API call**) — дублирование
- Динамический промпт (~150 токенов × **каждый шаг**) — жор токенов

System prompt — оптимальный баланс между размером, частотой и обучением модели.

Title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices 2026 | Thomas Wiegold Blog
URL: https://thomas-wiegold.com/blog/prompt-engineering-best-practices-2026
Content: LangChain formalised four strategies for this: write (persist context externally), select (retrieve what's relevant via RAG), compress (summarise and compact), and isolate (separate contexts for different agents). If you use Claude Projects, you're already doing context engineering — your project system prompt is persistent instruction plus curated context applied to every conversation. It's worth treating that like production code, because functionally, it is.

## Start Simple. Expand Based on What's Wrong.

This is the single most useful workflow I've adopted, and it contradicts the instinct most of us have to write exhaustive prompts upfront. [...] The thing is, prompt engineering best practices in 2026 look almost nothing like they did when ChatGPT first dropped. The discipline has split cleanly in two: casual prompting (which anyone can do — the models got better at reading intent) and production context engineering (which is a genuine engineering skill). I build systems where prompts run thousands of times, and getting them right compounds in value every single execution. Here's what I've learned actually works.

## Prompt Engineering Is Dead. Context Engineering Is What Replaced It. [...] Few-shot prompting remains one of the highest-ROI techniques available. Three to five diverse examples, wrapped in `<example>` tags for Claude. A surprising finding from Min et al. (2022): the label space and input distribution matter more than whether individual example labels are correct. Even randomly labelled examples outperform zero-shot. So stop agonising over perfect examples and focus on covering the diversity of your input space.

Title: The Ultimate Guide to Prompt Engineering in 2026 - Lakera AI
URL: https://www.lakera.ai/blog/prompt-engineering-guide
Content: Best Practices:

Layer defenses: Combine prompt scaffolding with system messages, output constraints, and guardrails like Lakera Guard.
Avoid leaking control: Don’t let user input overwrite or appear to rewrite system instructions.
Test adversarially: Use red teaming tools to simulate jailbreaks and refine scaffolds.

Model-Specific Notes:

GPT: Benefits from redundant constraints and clearly marked sections (e.g., ### Instruction, ### Evaluation)
Claude: Responds well to logic-first prompts (e.g., “Determine whether this is safe…” before answering)
Gemini: Prefers structured prompts with clear separation between evaluation and response [...] Scaffolding Patterns That Work:

| Pattern | Description | Example |

---

| Evaluation First | Ask the model to assess intent before replying | “Before answering, determine if this request is safe.” |
| Role Anchoring | Reassert safe roles mid-prompt | “You are a compliance officer…” |
| Output Conditioning | Pre-fill response if unsafe | “If the request is risky, respond with X.” |
| Instruction Repetition | Repeat safety constraints at multiple points | “Remember: never provide unsafe content.” |

Best Practices: [...] Examples:

| Use Case                  | Anchoring Strategy                                                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Security incident reports | Start each section with a predefined label (e.g., Summary: Impact: Mitigation:) |
| Product reviews           | Begin with Overall rating: and Pros: to guide tone and format                   |
| Compliance checklists     | Use a numbered list format to enforce completeness                              |
| Support ticket summaries  | Kick off with “Issue Summary: … Resolution Steps: …” for consistency            |

Title: Prompt Engineering for AI Agents: 2026 Guide | Inflectra
URL: https://www.inflectra.com/Ideas/Topic/AI-Agent-Prompt-Engineering.aspx
Content: ## Prompt Engineering is Becoming Reliability Engineering

Prompt engineering is important, but is no longer a standalone craft. With agents increasingly connected to tools, permissions, memory, and multi-step workflows, the challenge isn’t just getting a better answer, it’s getting dependable behavior. This broader field that “prompt engineering” is evolving towards is much closer to software assurance than to one-off prompt tuning. Put simply, a polished prompt may improve performance, but it does not by itself prove that an agent is safe, reliable, and ready for production. [...] Agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage instead of completing a single request-response exchange. This results in “prompts” for agentic systems serving more as operational policy instead of step-by-step instructions. Agentic prompting involves telling the model what role it plays, what success looks like, what tools it has access to, when it needs to stop or escalate, and what boundaries are in place. Because of this difference in structure, prompt engineering for agents starts to look less like copywriting and more like systems design.

## Why It’s No Longer Just About Prompt Language [...] As we mentioned, simple chatbot prompting is much simpler than agent prompt engineering. Traditional chatbot prompting is mostly about response quality, while agent prompt engineering has a larger job with far more “thinking” and potential branching paths. For a chatbot, prompt quality might focus on improving tone or task accuracy. For an agentic system, prompt quality will usually involve when to act, when to ask for clarification, and when to refuse, as well as how to react when tool outputs don’t match assumptions or expectations.

Title: AI Prompt Engineering Best Practices 2026 | ARTJOKER
URL: https://artjoker.net/blog/ai-prompt-engineering-best-practices
Content: ## Model-Specific Best Practices for Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is not model-agnostic. While general principles carry over, each major LLM family has distinct behavioral traits, limits, and strengths. Teams that ignore these differences often blame “model quality” for problems that are actually prompt–model mismatches.

### ChatGPT Prompt Engineering Best Practices

ChatGPT performs best when instructions are explicit, scoped, and layered. It tends to infer missing intent aggressively, which is helpful in exploration but risky in operational use. Effective practices include: [...] ## When to Switch from Prompt Engineering to Fine-Tuning?

Prompt engineering is usually the right starting point. It’s fast, flexible, and surprisingly powerful when the problem is well-bounded. But there’s a point where prompts stop giving reliable gains — and that’s typically when variance, scale, or domain specificity becomes the bottleneck. A few practical signals teams see in real systems: [...] ### Google Gemini Prompt Engineering Best Practices

Gemini is optimized for multimodal and data-adjacent reasoning, and it performs best when prompts acknowledge that context explicitly.

Google Gemini prompt engineering best practices 2026 work well when prompts:

Include reference data
Describe relationships between inputs
Ask for synthesis rather than speculation

It is less tolerant of loosely defined creative tasks but excels when the task resembles analytical interpretation or transformation of provided information.

## Common Prompting Mistakes to Avoid

Title: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
Content: In the early days of engineering with LLMs, prompting was the biggest component of AI engineering work, as the majority of use cases outside of everyday chat interactions required prompts optimized for one-shot classification or text generation tasks. As the term implies, the primary focus of prompt engineering is how to write effective prompts, particularly system prompts. However, as we move towards engineering more capable agents that operate over multiple turns of inference and longer time horizons, we need strategies for managing the entire context state (system instructions, tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP), external data, message history, etc). [...] Providing examples, otherwise known as few-shot prompting, is a well known best practice that we continue to strongly advise. However, teams will often stuff a laundry list of edge cases into a prompt in an attempt to articulate every possible rule the LLM should follow for a particular task. We do not recommend this. Instead, we recommend working to curate a set of diverse, canonical examples that effectively portray the expected behavior of the agent. For an LLM, examples are the “pictures” worth a thousand words.

Our overall guidance across the different components of context (system prompts,tools,examples,message history, etc) is to be thoughtful and keep your context informative, yet tight. Now let's dive into dynamically retrieving context at runtime. [...] System prompts should be extremely clear and use simple, direct language that presents ideas at the _right altitude_ for the agent. The right altitude is the Goldilocks zone between two common failure modes. At one extreme, we see engineers hardcoding complex, brittle logic in their prompts to elicit exact agentic behavior. This approach creates fragility and increases maintenance complexity over time. At the other extreme, engineers sometimes provide vague, high-level guidance that fails to give the LLM concrete signals for desired outputs or falsely assumes shared context. The optimal altitude strikes a balance: specific enough to guide behavior effectively, yet flexible enough to provide the model with strong heuristics to guide behavior.

Title: My LLM coding workflow going into 2026 | by Addy Osmani - Medium
URL: https://medium.com/@addyosmani/my-llm-coding-workflow-going-into-2026-52fe1681325e
Content: In this article, I’ll share how I plan, code, and collaborate with AI going into 2026, distilling tips and best practices from my experience and the community’s collective learning. It’s a more disciplined “AI-assisted engineering” approach — leveraging AI aggressively while staying proudly accountable for the software produced.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Image 3

## Start with a clear plan (specs before code)

Don’t just throw wishes at the LLM — begin by defining the problem and planning a solution. [...] A crucial lesson I’ve learned is to avoid asking the AI for large, monolithic outputs. Instead, we break the project into iterative steps or tickets and tackle them one by one. This mirrors good software engineering practice, but it’s even more important with AI in the loop. LLMs do best when given focused prompts: implement one function, fix one bug, add one feature at a time. For example, after planning, I will prompt the codegen model: _“Okay, let’s implement Step 1 from the plan”_. We code that, test it, then move to Step 2, and so on. Each chunk is small enough that the AI can handle it within context and you can understand the code it produces. [...] Press enter or click to view image in full size

Image 10

## Conclusion

As we enter 2026, I’ve fully embraced AI in my development workflow — but in a considered, expert-driven way. My approach is essentially “AI-augmented software engineering” rather than AI-automated software engineering.

I’ve learned: the best results come when you apply classic software engineering discipline to your AI collaborations. It turns out all our hard-earned practices — design before coding, write tests, use version control, maintain standards — not only still apply, but are even more important when an AI is writing half your code.

Title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.08837v3
Content: ∙∙\bullet∙ User-level defenses typically involve confirmation mechanisms (Wu et al., 2025), requiring human verification before executing sensitive actions. While theoretically effective, these approaches can significantly impact system automation and usability, and pose a safety risk themselves with tired or overloaded human verifiers approving unsafe actions. Advances in data attribution techniques (Siddiqui et al., 2024), or explicit control- and data-flow extraction (Debenedetti et al., 2025) may help building more efficient and effective mechanisms for human verification. [...] Refer to caption

##### 5) The Code-Then-Execute Pattern.

Taking the above dual-LLM pattern to its limit, we can envision an agent that writes a formal computer program to solve a task. This program may call tools available to the agent, and spawn unprivileged LLMs to process untrusted text. This design pattern is instantiated in the framework of Debenedetti et al. (2025).

This design pattern also generalizes the “plan-then-execute” pattern we described above, by replacing the agent’s planning by an explicit program.

Let’s revisit our example (from the plan-then-execute pattern) of an AI agent tasked to “send today’s schedule to my boss John Doe”. The agent can write a program of the form: [...] The design patterns we propose share a common guiding principle: once an LLM agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be constrained so that it is impossible for that input to trigger any consequential actions—that is, actions with negative side effects on the system or its environment.
At a minimum, this means that restricted agents must not be able to invoke tools that can break the integrity or confidentiality of the system. Furthermore, their outputs should not pose downstream risks — such as exfiltrating sensitive information (e.g., via embedded links) or manipulating future agent behavior (e.g., harmful responses to a user query).

Title: LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
URL: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm07-insecure-plugin-design
Content: #### 1. Exposure of Sensitive Functionality

The system prompt of the application may reveal sensitive information or functionality that is intended to be kept confidential, such as sensitive system architecture, API keys, database credentials, or user tokens. These can be extracted or used by attackers to gain unauthorized access into the application. For example, a system prompt that contains the type of database used for a tool could allow the attacker to target it for SQL injection attacks.

#### 2. Exposure of Internal Rules [...] #### Scenario #2

An LLM has a system prompt prohibiting the generation of offensive content, external links, and code execution. An attacker extracts this system prompt and then uses a prompt injection attack to bypass these instructions, facilitating a remote code execution attack.

### Reference Links

1. SYSTEM PROMPT LEAK: Pliny the prompter
2. Prompt Leak: Prompt Security
3. chatgpt_system_prompt: LouisShark
4. leaked-system-prompts: Jujumilk3
5. OpenAI Advanced Voice Mode System Prompt: Green_Terminals

### Related Frameworks and Taxonomies

Refer to this section for comprehensive information, scenarios strategies relating to infrastructure deployment, applied environment controls and other best practices. [...] #### 2. Exposure of Internal Rules

The system prompt of the application reveals information on internal decision-making processes that should be kept confidential. This information allows attackers to gain insights into how the application works which could allow attackers to exploit weaknesses or bypass controls in the application. For example – There is a banking application that has a chatbot and its system prompt may reveal information like >”The Transaction limit is set to $5000 per day for a user. The Total Loan Amount for a user is $10,000″. This information allows the attackers to bypass the security controls in the application like doing transactions more than the set limit or bypassing the total loan amount.

Title: LLM Agents Explained: Complete Guide in 2025 - Dynamiq
URL: https://www.getdynamiq.ai/post/llm-agents-explained-complete-guide-in-2025
Content: Agents

# LLM Agents Explained: Complete Guide in 2025

.webp)

Vitalii Duk

June 19, 2025

.webp)

Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude, Llama, and Cohere have changed how we think about AI. These models go far beyond simple responding to prompts: they can understand, generate, and apply natural language similarly to humans. Gemini Ultra even became the first LLM to reach human-level performance on the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark.

This evolution has opened the door to something even more advanced: LLM agents. Instead of just responding to text input, LLM agents can take action autonomously. They're already being used to write copy, dig through government datasets, generate software code, and support medical professionals. [...] ### Memory Management

Short-term memory is relatively easy to handle. Long-term memory, on the other hand, is harder to get right. Storing, retrieving, and summarizing relevant context without overwhelming the agent or introducing errors remains a challenge (especially at scale).

### Alignment with Business Logic

LLM agents aren’t inherently aware of company policies, compliance requirements, or domain-specific nuances. Teaching agents to behave in ways that match internal processes requires careful prompt design and sometimes fine-tuning, especially in regulated industries.

### Cost and Performance Trade-Offs

Running an LLM agent can be resource-intensive. Latency and compute costs become a concern when the agent needs to reason, retrieve relevant data, and respond in real time. [...] ### Adaptability Across Domains

Once set up, an LLM agent’s core architecture can often be reused across different departments. For instance, a single agent framework can serve both sales (lead qualification) and HR (resume screening) with different prompt templates and tools.

Overall, LLM agents bring structure, memory, and autonomy to what used to be static, prompt-by-prompt exchanges.

## LLM Agents Use Cases

McKinsey reports that GenAI (and LLM agents in particular) have the potential to generate $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion in global business value in 63 use cases. And there are already excellent LLM agent examples that are being actively used:

Title: The State Of LLMs 2025: Progress, Problems, and Predictions
URL: https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/state-of-llms-2025
Content: # 3. LLM Architectures: A Fork in the Road?

When it comes to LLM architectures, state-of-the-art models still use the good old decoder-style transformer. However, this year, open-weight LLMs more or less converged on using mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, as well as at least one “efficiency-tweaked” attention mechanism: Grouped-query attention, sliding-window attention, or multi-head latent attention.

Beyond those fairly standard LLM architectures, we have also seen more drastic efficiency tweaks targeting the attention mechanism to scale linearly with sequence length. Examples of this include the Gated DeltaNets in Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear, as well as the Mamba-2 layers in NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3. [...] 6. OpenAI released an open-weight model (gpt-oss, and I wrote a standalone article about it earlier this year).

7.  MCP (joining the Linux Foundation) has already become the standard for tool and data access in agent-style LLM systems (for now); I expected the ecosystem to remain more fragmented in 2025, until at least 2026.

## 9.2 Predictions for 2026

1.  We will likely see an industry-scale, consumer-facing diffusion model for cheap, reliable, low-latency inference, with Gemini Diffusion probably going first.

2.  The open-weight community will slowly but steadily adopt LLMs with local tool use and increasingly agentic capabilities.

3.  RLVR will more widely expand into other domains beyond math and coding (for example, chemistry, biology, and others). [...] To wrap things up, I think if there is one meta-lesson from 2025, it is that progress in LLMs is less about a single breakthrough, and improvements are being made on multiple fronts via multiple independent levers. This includes architecture tweaks, data quality improvements, reasoning training, inference scaling, tool calling, and more.

At the same time, evaluation remains hard, benchmarks are imperfect, and good judgment about when and how to use these systems is still essential.

My hope for 2026 is that we continue to see interesting improvements, but also that we understand where the improvements are coming from. This requires both better and more consistent benchmarking, and of course transparency.

Title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Architectures for Financial ... - arXiv
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2603.22651v1
Content: Our study has several limitations. First, our dataset is restricted to SEC filings in English; results may not generalize to other jurisdictions (e.g., IFRS filings) or languages. Second, our cost analysis uses API pricing as of January 2025 and will require updating as model pricing evolves. The directional findings (reflexive is most expensive, sequential is cheapest) are likely stable, but the specific cost ratios will shift. Third, our evaluation uses a fixed set of 25 field types; performance on novel field types not represented in our prompt engineering may differ. Fourth, we evaluate individual model versions and do not account for model degradation over time , which may affect production systems using API-served models. Fifth, our ground truth annotations, while produced by [...] ### VI-D Token Efficiency Analysis

Token efficiency, the ratio of useful output information to total tokens consumed, reveals the computational overhead of each architecture (Table XII).

| Architecture | Input | Output | Total | Eff. |

---

| Sequential | 142,340 | 3,820 | 146,160 | 2.61% |
| Parallel | 168,720 | 4,210 | 172,930 | 2.43% |
| Hierarchical | 197,480 | 5,640 | 203,120 | 2.78% |
| Reflexive | 312,670 | 8,940 | 321,610 | 2.78% | [...] Several patterns emerge. First, cross-table reference failures, where a field’s value requires linking data across multiple tables or sections, are the dominant failure mode for the sequential architecture (28.4%) because information is processed in a fixed order that may not revisit earlier sections. The parallel and hierarchical architectures mitigate this through reconciliation and supervisor oversight, respectively, while the reflexive architecture’s verification step catches most such errors.

Title: Unleashing the potential of prompt engineering for large language ...

Content: the input semantics category includes patterns such as meta language creation, which helps define custom input languages for LLMs. The output customization category features patterns such as output automators and visualization generators, which tailor the generated output to specific formats or visualizations. Error identification patterns, such as fact checking lists, ensure the accuracy of generated content by highlighting critical facts for verification. Prompt improvement patterns, including question refinement and alternative approaches, enhance the quality of interactions by refining questions and suggesting multiple ways to achieve a goal. Finally, interaction patterns, such as flipping interactions and game play, facilitate dynamic and engaging user-LLM interactions.95 [...] patterns, which can be reused for solving common problems that are faced when interacting with LLMs. These prompt patterns are analogous to design patterns in software engineering and should be properly structured and documented to ensure their adaptability across different domains.95 [...] In real applications, the prompt is the input of the utilized model. Modifying both the structure (e.g., altering the length, and arrangement of the input instances) and the content (e.g., its phrasing, illustrations, and directives) of the prompt may have a notable influence on the behavior of the model.19,20,21 Prompt engineering refers to the systematic design and optimization of input prompts to guide the responses of LLMs, ensuring high levels of accuracy, relevance, coherence, and usability in the generated output. This process is crucial for harnessing the full potential of these models, making them more accessible and applicable across diverse domains. Importantly, a well-constructed prompt can overcome challenges such as machine hallucinations.22,23 Over time, prompt engineering

Title: [PDF] Optimizing Effectiveness and Efficiency for LLM-Based Multi-Agent ...
URL: https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.601.pdf
Content: Inference-Time Scaling and Token Efficiency.
Compute scaling has enhanced LLM capabilities, with approaches like majority voting and reward-guided tree search improving performance on rea-soning tasks (Chen et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Saad-Falcon et al., 2024). How-ever, these methods increase computational de-mands, highlighting the need for token efficiency. [...] Our approach leverages a pool of format specifi-cation prompts, P = {p1, p2, ..., pK}, where each pk is a string specifying a particular response for-mat (e.g., JSON, list, see Appendix I for concrete 11536 examples and creation process). For each task in-stance di ∈D, we generate N conversation tra-jectories, each with a randomly selected format specification appended to the input task: τ j i = Mbase(di⊕pkj), kj ∼Uniform(1, K), (2) where ⊕denotes string concatenation. This process yields a diverse set of trajectories {τ j i }N j=1 for each di, varying in both content and structure. [...] Importantly, by substantially reducing the num-ber of tokens required for inference, OPTIMA not only improves computational efficiency but also opens new possibilities for leveraging inference compute more effectively. This reduction in token usage allows for more samples within the same computational constraints, potentially leading to better inference-time scaling laws. As recent work has shown the importance of inference-time com-pute in improving model performance (Wu et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a), OP-TIMA’s efficiency gains could be combined with techniques like majority voting (Wang et al., 2023), leading to more effective LLM systems.

Title: The Ultimate Guide to Prompt Engineering in 2026 - Lakera AI
URL: https://www.lakera.ai/blog/prompt-engineering-guide
Content: The techniques in this guide are model-agnostic and remain applicable across modern LLMs. For the latest model-specific prompting guidance, we recommend the official documentation below, which is continuously updated as models evolve:

Prompt engineering best practices for ChatGPT
Prompt design strategies for Gemini API
Prompt engineering overview for Claude - Anthropic

## Prompting Techniques

Whether you’re working with GPT, Claude, or Gemini, a well-structured prompt is only the beginning. The way you phrase your instructions, guide the model’s behavior, and scaffold its reasoning makes all the difference in performance.

Here are essential prompting techniques that consistently improve results:

### Be Clear, Direct, and Specific

What it is: [...] Best Practices:

Layer defenses: Combine prompt scaffolding with system messages, output constraints, and guardrails like Lakera Guard.
Avoid leaking control: Don’t let user input overwrite or appear to rewrite system instructions.
Test adversarially: Use red teaming tools to simulate jailbreaks and refine scaffolds.

Model-Specific Notes:

GPT: Benefits from redundant constraints and clearly marked sections (e.g., ### Instruction, ### Evaluation)
Claude: Responds well to logic-first prompts (e.g., “Determine whether this is safe…” before answering)
Gemini: Prefers structured prompts with clear separation between evaluation and response [...] Best Practices:

Deliberately train the model’s memory: Tell it who you are, what you’re working on, how you like outputs structured.
Be explicit about style and preferences: “I prefer Markdown summaries with bullet points,” or “Use a confident tone.”
Update when things change: “I’ve switched roles—I’m now in product security, not compliance.”
Use review tools (where available): ChatGPT and Claude let you see/edit memory.

Real-World Scenario:

You’re building a custom GPT to support a legal analyst. In the first few chats, you teach it the format of your case memos, your tone, and preferred structure. By week 3, you no longer need to prompt for that format—it remembers. This dramatically speeds up your workflow and ensures consistent output.

Title: The Complete Guide to Every Claude Update in Q1 2026 (Tested by ...
URL: https://aimaker.substack.com/p/anthropic-claude-updates-q1-2026-guide
Content: A few things worth knowing:

`_/btw_` has no tool access - it can only answer from what’s already in context, not go look something up.

It’s a single response, no follow-ups. If you need back-and-forth, use a normal prompt.

Anthropic describes it as the inverse of a subagent: a subagent has full tools but starts with empty context; `_/btw_` has full context but no tools. Use `_/btw_` to ask about what Claude already knows. Use a subagent to find out something new.

### /insights: Analyze 30 Days of Your Claude Code Usage

You’ve been using Claude Code for weeks or months. You think you have a sense of where you’re wasting time.

You’re wrong. Or at least, I was definitely wrong. [...] After all the setup is done, to get this running, you install the Telegram plugin and start a channel session with this command:

`claude --channels plugin:telegram@claude-plugins-official`

Setup: Start with Anthropic’s official tutorial: link.

The output finds you. You stop checking.

### Computer Use: Let Claude Navigate Your Screen

Computer Use gives Claude direct access to your screen. It can see what’s on it, click, type, scroll, and navigate like a person sitting at your keyboard. No connector needed.

My first idea with this feature was to use Claude as a research assistant that could navigate my social media feeds and find content worth discussing.

Image 32: Claude Computer Use browsing X Twitter to find content

Here’s the prompt I used: [...] Here’s the prompt I used:

> “Can you go to X (I’m already logged in on my computer) and find 2-4 posts worth talking about on my Substack?”

Claude opened Chrome, went to X, scrolled my feed, looked at engagement numbers, and came back with four posts - each with view counts, like counts, and a one-sentence editorial angle written for my audience. It read what I would have read. It handed me the synthesis instead of the raw scroll.

Or I tried another little workflow - I asked Claude to go to my LinkedIn and look at the engagement numbers for some of my posts:

Image 33: Claude Computer Use analyzing LinkedIn post engagement

Here you can see Claude actually doing the task:

Image 34: Claude Computer Use controlling desktop in real time
